content:
By winter, I knew the difference between the way each of them reached for me in the dark.

Aang’s touch arrived like a question.

Even after months together, even after kisses that had long since stopped being tentative, he still gave me that half-breath of space where I could lean closer or not. His fingers would brush mine beneath blankets, warm and restless, and wait.

Katara’s touch was deliberate.

A palm at the center of my back. Fingers around my wrist when she wanted my attention. A thumb against my cheek after she had already read my expression and decided I was pretending not to need comfort.

Toph did not reach so much as occupy.

A foot over mine beneath the table. Her shoulder shoved under my arm. Her head dropped into my lap with no warning while she complained that affection was stupid and then became personally offended if I stopped touching her hair.

I loved all three languages.

That was why I noticed when touch disappeared.

It began after the threats.

Nobody meant to change.

Aang simply started scanning crowds more often before taking my hand.

Katara checked the locks twice each night.

Toph began walking on the street side whenever we were together, body angled toward every unfamiliar vibration.

Care became vigilance.

Vigilance became distance.

The first time I reached for Aang in the market and he looked over my shoulder before looking at me, I let my hand fall.

He did not notice.

That hurt more than it should have.

For two days I said nothing.

We had, apparently, learned some lessons more slowly than others.

The third evening, snow began falling over Cranefish Town.

Not much. A thin, uncertain dusting that melted against factory roofs and clung to the old stone walls.

Katara stood in the courtyard smiling up at it.

“You miss home,” I said.

She caught one flake on her palm.

“Sometimes.”

Toph came outside barefoot.

Katara stared at her feet.

“No.”

“What?”

“Shoes.”

“I can’t see through shoes.”

“You can get frostbite through stubbornness.”

“Prove it.”

Katara produced water from her flask.

Toph immediately retreated inside.

Aang laughed.

For the first time in days, the sound loosened something in me.

We ended up in the sitting room with every cushion dragged to the floor. Aang lit the brazier. Katara made spiced tea. Toph complained about winter until Katara put both of Toph’s feet under a heated blanket and received no further objections.

It should have been comfortable.

Instead I sat at the edge of the cushions with my cup between both hands.

Aang looked at me.

This time he saw it.

“What’s wrong?”

There were four possible bad answers and one useful one.

I chose the useful one with difficulty.

“I miss being touched without it being about keeping me safe.”

The room went still.

Toph’s head turned.

Katara’s eyes widened.

Aang looked stricken.

I kept going before any of them could apologize me out of the feeling.

“I know why it changed. I know the notes scared you. They scared me too. But I feel like every time we’re outside, you’re guarding me. And every time we’re home, you’re recovering from guarding me.”

Katara set down her cup.

“Oh.”

Not defensive.

Not dismissive.

Just understanding arriving painfully.

Aang looked at his hands. “I didn’t realize.”

“I know.”

Toph said, “I did.”

We all looked at her.

She shrugged.

“Your heartbeat changes when somebody grabs you in crowds now.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?” Katara asked.

Toph’s expression sharpened. “Because it’s their heartbeat.”

That answer was so perfectly Toph that nobody argued.

I took a breath.

“I don’t want you to stop paying attention to danger.”

Aang nodded.

“I want danger to stop getting all the meaning.”

Katara moved first.

Slowly.

She held out her hand between us.

Not touching.

Offering.

I set my cup aside and put my hand in hers.

Her fingers closed around mine.

Warm.

No crisis.

No crowd.

No purpose beyond wanting contact.

Aang shifted closer on my other side.

“Can I?”

I smiled.

“Yes.”

He leaned his shoulder against mine.

Toph made a disgusted noise.

Then she crawled across the cushions and dropped her head into my lap.

“There. Everybody happy?”

Katara laughed.

I ran my fingers lightly over Toph’s hair.

She immediately relaxed and pretended not to.

The evening changed after that.

Not into anything dramatic.

That was the point.

Aang traced circles against the inside of my wrist while telling a story about Monk Gyatso cheating at Pai Sho. Katara’s legs tangled with mine under the blanket. Toph stole my tea and gave it back after deciding it was too sweet.

Touch stopped being evidence that something might happen.

It became what was happening.

Later, kisses replaced conversation.

Aang tasted faintly of cinnamon.

Katara laughed against my mouth when I tried to pull the blanket higher and accidentally trapped Toph underneath it.

Toph emerged swearing, grabbed the front of my shirt, and kissed me hard enough to make Aang choke on his own laugh.

“Subtle,” Katara said.

“Waste of time.”

The room warmed beyond anything the brazier could explain.

Hands wandered, then stopped, then asked.

Yes.

Not yet.

Here.

Slower.

Again.

The words did not break the mood. They built it.

At some point Aang blew out the lamps with a curl of air and Toph complained that this gave everyone else an unfair advantage.

“You literally function better in the dark,” I said.

“That’s not the point.”

Katara kissed her quiet.

Toph made a surprised sound.

I would treasure it forever.

What followed belonged to us.

Not because bodies were shameful.

Because privacy was one of the few luxuries the world had not managed to tax, legislate, publish, or turn into a statement about the Avatar.

There was laughter.

There was awkwardness.

There were pauses when somebody needed water or had an elbow in the wrong place or discovered that four adults under one blanket required strategy.

There was tenderness so intense it made me want to hide from it and move closer at the same time.

Afterward, snow pressed pale light against the windows.

Aang lay on the rug with his head against Katara’s stomach. Toph had claimed half my chest as a pillow. Katara’s fingers moved lazily through Aang’s hair.

Nobody looked heroic.

Thank the spirits.

Aang’s eyes were half closed.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“For what?”

“For making care feel like surveillance.”

Katara exhaled. “Me too.”

Toph’s voice came muffled against me. “I’m not sorry.”

I looked down.

She lifted one eyebrow.

“I’m adjusting.”

That was Toph for “I heard you.”

I kissed the top of her head.

She bit my shoulder through the blanket.

“That seems counterproductive.”

“Affection.”

“Terrifying.”

Katara smiled.

I looked at the three of them.

Love was made visible by touch, sometimes.

But touch was not proof of love by itself.

It mattered because of the space around it.

The pause before Aang’s hand closed over mine.

The way Katara could hold me firmly without deciding for me.

The way Toph could lean her whole weight into my body because she trusted I would tell her if I wanted space.

Consent lived there.

So did safety.

Not in never being afraid.

In knowing fear did not own every gesture after it arrived.

Outside, the city disappeared slowly beneath snow.

Inside, nobody kept watch for a while.

The quiet after fear became its own kind of intimacy.

For several nights, none of us wanted anything complicated from one another. No dramatic declarations. No new boundaries to negotiate. We slept, woke, worked, and found small ways back into our bodies.

Katara braided the loose cord on my sleeve while we sat by the stove. Aang rested with his head in her lap, eyes closed, listening to Toph complain about a student who had tried to invent “freestyle metalbending” and nearly trapped himself in a cabinet.

“He had vision,” Aang murmured.

“He had a concussion.”

“Both can be true.”

Toph threw a cushion. Aang caught it without opening his eyes.

I laughed, and the sound surprised me.

Katara’s fingers paused against my wrist. “There you are.”

The words almost broke me.

Not because I had been gone. Because some part of me had believed I needed to return all at once.

I covered her hand with mine.

Later, in bed, Aang asked before pulling me closer. Katara asked whether I wanted the lamp out. Toph asked nothing, but her foot found mine beneath the blankets and waited there until I pressed back.

Consent was not always a formal question. Sometimes it was making space large enough for an answer.

The threat had made every unexpected sound feel like an intrusion.

This was how we reclaimed touch: slowly enough that nobody had to pretend bravery.

Snow brushed the window.

Aang’s breathing evened first. Katara’s followed. Toph muttered something insulting in her sleep.

I smiled into the dark.

The room was not safe because danger had ceased to exist.

It was safe because fear was allowed to exist here without becoming the only thing we could feel.
